claim: Impairments of locus coeruleus (LC) are implicated in anxiety/depression and Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Impairments of locus coeruleus (LC) are implicated in anxiety/depression and Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about LC involvement in these conditions.

claim: Increases in cytosolic noradrenaline (NA) concentration and monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) activity initiate the LC impairment through production of NA metabolite, 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl-glycolaldehyde (DOPEGAL), by MAO-A.
source: Increases in cytosolic noradrenaline (NA) concentration and monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) activity initiate the LC impairment through production of NA metabolite, 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl-glycolaldehyde (DOPEGAL), by MAO-A.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing Burke et al., 1999 and other studies.

claim: NA is virtually absent in cytosol while NA is produced exclusively in cytoplasmic vesicles from dopamine by dopamine-β-hydroxylase.
source: However, how NA accumulates in soma/dendritic cytosol of LC neurons has never been addressed despite the fact that NA is virtually absent in cytosol while NA is produced exclusively in cytoplasmic vesicles from dopamine by dopamine-β-hydroxylase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Potter and Axelrod, 1963 in the introduction and represents established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Reuptake of autocrine-released NA following spike activity is the major source of NA accumulation.
source: Since reuptake of autocrine-released NA following spike activity is the major source of NA accumulation, we investigated whether and how chronic stress can increase the spike activity accompanied by NA autocrine.
evidence: This is stated as a premise in the abstract and is supported by citation to Torres et al., 2003 in the introduction.

claim: Overexcitation of LC neurons is normally prevented by the autoinhibition mediated by activation of α2A-adrenergic receptor (AR)-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium-current (GIRK-I) with autocrine-released NA.
source: Overexcitation of LC neurons is normally prevented by the autoinhibition mediated by activation of α2A-adrenergic receptor (AR)-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium-current (GIRK-I) with autocrine-released NA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Williams et al., 1985, Arima et al., 1998, and other studies in the introduction.

claim: NA-induced GIRK-I in LC neurons was decreased in chronic restraint stress (RS) mice.
source: Patch-clamp study revealed that NA-induced GIRK-I in LC neurons was decreased in chronic restraint stress (RS) mice, while a similar decrease was gradually caused by repeated excitation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-G.

claim: A similar decrease in NA-induced GIRK-I was gradually caused by repeated excitation.
source: Patch-clamp study revealed that NA-induced GIRK-I in LC neurons was decreased in chronic restraint stress (RS) mice, while a similar decrease was gradually caused by repeated excitation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Chronic RS caused internalization of α2A-ARs expressed in cell membrane in LC neurons.
source: Chronic RS caused internalization of α2A-ARs expressed in cell membrane in LC neurons and decreased protein/mRNA levels of α2A-ARs/GIRKs in membrane fraction.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical and western blot data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Chronic RS decreased protein/mRNA levels of α2A-ARs/GIRKs in membrane fraction.
source: Chronic RS caused internalization of α2A-ARs expressed in cell membrane in LC neurons and decreased protein/mRNA levels of α2A-ARs/GIRKs in membrane fraction.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Chronic RS increased the protein levels of MAO-A.
source: Subsequently, chronic RS increased the protein levels of MAO-A, DOPEGAL-induced asparagine endopeptidase (AEP), and tau N368.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: Chronic RS increased the protein levels of DOPEGAL-induced asparagine endopeptidase (AEP).
source: Subsequently, chronic RS increased the protein levels of MAO-A, DOPEGAL-induced asparagine endopeptidase (AEP), and tau N368.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Chronic RS increased the protein levels of tau N368.
source: Subsequently, chronic RS increased the protein levels of MAO-A, DOPEGAL-induced asparagine endopeptidase (AEP), and tau N368.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: Internalization of α2A-AR increased cytosolic NA by facilitating reuptake of autocrine-released NA.
source: Thus, it is likely that internalization of α2A-AR increased cytosolic NA, as reflected in AEP increases, by facilitating reuptake of autocrine-released NA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 6.

claim: The suppression of α2A-AR internalization may have a translational potential for anxiety/AD treatment.
source: The suppression of α2A-AR internalization may have a translational potential for anxiety/AD treatment.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: Locus coeruleus (LC) is implicated in anxiety and depression.
source: Locus coeruleus (LC) is implicated in anxiety and depression (Itoi and Sugimoto, 2010) and is often the first place where Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related pathology appears (Mather and Harley, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Itoi and Sugimoto, 2010.

claim: LC is often the first place where Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related pathology appears.
source: Locus coeruleus (LC) is implicated in anxiety and depression (Itoi and Sugimoto, 2010) and is often the first place where Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related pathology appears (Mather and Harley, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mather and Harley, 2016.

claim: Noradrenaline (NA) is known to inhibit amyloid-induced oxidative stress and caspase activation in cortex/hippocampus.
source: Noradrenaline (NA) is known to inhibit amyloid-induced oxidative stress and caspase activation in cortex/hippocampus (Counts and Mufson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Counts and Mufson, 2010.

claim: The impairment of the LC-noradrenergic system is potentially involved in the AD pathogenesis.
source: Thus, the impairment of the LC-noradrenergic system is potentially involved in the AD pathogenesis (Ross et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ross et al., 2015 and Chen et al., 2022.

claim: Cytosolic NA in the soma/dendrites of LC neurons is degraded by monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) into 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl-glycolaldehyde (DOPEGAL).
source: It was reported that cytosolic NA in the soma/dendrites of LC neurons is degraded by monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) into 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl-glycolaldehyde (DOPEGAL) (Burke et al., 1999), which generates apoptotic free radicals (Burke et al., 1998) and activates asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) to produce Aβ and hyperphosphorylated tau, consequently leading to AD (Burke et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burke et al., 1999.

claim: DOPEGAL generates apoptotic free radicals.
source: It was reported that cytosolic NA in the soma/dendrites of LC neurons is degraded by monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) into 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl-glycolaldehyde (DOPEGAL) (Burke et al., 1999), which generates apoptotic free radicals (Burke et al., 1998) and activates asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) to produce Aβ and hyperphosphorylated tau, consequently leading to AD (Burke et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burke et al., 1998.

claim: DOPEGAL activates asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) to produce Aβ and hyperphosphorylated tau, consequently leading to AD.
source: It was reported that cytosolic NA in the soma/dendrites of LC neurons is degraded by monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A) into 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl-glycolaldehyde (DOPEGAL) (Burke et al., 1999), which generates apoptotic free radicals (Burke et al., 1998) and activates asparagine endopeptidase (AEP) to produce Aβ and hyperphosphorylated tau, consequently leading to AD (Burke et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burke et al., 1999 and Kang et al., 2020.

claim: There normally appears to be no NA except dopamine in the cytosol of LC neurons because NA is produced exclusively in cytoplasmic vesicles by dopamine-β-hydroxylase (DBH).
source: However, there normally appears to be no NA except dopamine in the cytosol of LC neurons because NA is produced exclusively in cytoplasmic vesicles by dopamine-β-hydroxylase (DBH) (Potter and Axelrod, 1963) from dopamine which is taken up into cytoplasmic vesicles by vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Potter and Axelrod, 1963.

claim: Dopamine is taken up into cytoplasmic vesicles by vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT2).
source: However, there normally appears to be no NA except dopamine in the cytosol of LC neurons because NA is produced exclusively in cytoplasmic vesicles by dopamine-β-hydroxylase (DBH) (Potter and Axelrod, 1963) from dopamine which is taken up into cytoplasmic vesicles by vesicular monoamine transporter type 2 (VMAT2).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about vesicular monoamine transport.

claim: LC neurons release NA following action potential not only from the axon terminals but also from their cell bodies as autocrine.
source: LC neurons release NA following action potential not only from the axon terminals but also from their cell bodies as autocrine (Huang et al., 2007), and autocrine-released NA activates α2A adrenergic receptor (α2A-AR) expressed on the soma/dendrites (Aoki et al., 1994), resulting in activation of α2-AR-coupled inwardly rectifying K+ (GIRK) channel (Arima et al., 1998) to cause autoinhibition (spike-afterhyperpolarization) (Williams et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2007.

claim: Autocrine-released NA activates α2A adrenergic receptor (α2A-AR) expressed on the soma/dendrites.
source: LC neurons release NA following action potential not only from the axon terminals but also from their cell bodies as autocrine (Huang et al., 2007), and autocrine-released NA activates α2A adrenergic receptor (α2A-AR) expressed on the soma/dendrites (Aoki et al., 1994), resulting in activation of α2-AR-coupled inwardly rectifying K+ (GIRK) channel (Arima et al., 1998) to cause autoinhibition (spike-afterhyperpolarization) (Williams et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aoki et al., 1994.

claim: Activation of α2A-AR results in activation of α2-AR-coupled inwardly rectifying K+ (GIRK) channel to cause autoinhibition (spike-afterhyperpolarization).
source: LC neurons release NA following action potential not only from the axon terminals but also from their cell bodies as autocrine (Huang et al., 2007), and autocrine-released NA activates α2A adrenergic receptor (α2A-AR) expressed on the soma/dendrites (Aoki et al., 1994), resulting in activation of α2-AR-coupled inwardly rectifying K+ (GIRK) channel (Arima et al., 1998) to cause autoinhibition (spike-afterhyperpolarization) (Williams et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arima et al., 1998 and Williams et al., 1985.

claim: Autocrine-released NA is taken up by NA transporter (NAT).
source: As autocrine-released NA is taken up by NA transporter (NAT) (Torres et al., 2003), uptaken-NA may be the only source of free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A in the cytosol of LC neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Torres et al., 2003.

claim: Uptaken-NA may be the only source of free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A in the cytosol of LC neurons.
source: As autocrine-released NA is taken up by NA transporter (NAT) (Torres et al., 2003), uptaken-NA may be the only source of free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A in the cytosol of LC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biochemical pathway and cited literature.

claim: The amount of free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A in the cytosol is thought to be very small due to a much lower affinity of NA to MAO-A compared to VMAT2.
source: However, the amount of free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A in the cytosol is thought to be very small due to a much lower affinity of NA to MAO-A compared to VMAT2 (Costa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Costa et al., 2012.

claim: The passive NA leakage occurs from cytoplasmic vesicles in a manner that achieves a dynamic equilibrium with active NA storage into cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2.
source: Because the passive NA leakage occurs from cytoplasmic vesicles in a manner that achieves a dynamic equilibrium with active NA storage into cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2 (Eisenhofer et al., 2004), increased NA uptake by NAT in response to increased NA autocrine following [Ca2+]i increases or overexcitation may increase free NA by facilitating the passive NA leakage from cytoplasmic vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eisenhofer et al., 2004.

claim: Increased NA uptake by NAT in response to increased NA autocrine following [Ca2+]i increases or overexcitation may increase free NA by facilitating the passive NA leakage from cytoplasmic vesicles.
source: Because the passive NA leakage occurs from cytoplasmic vesicles in a manner that achieves a dynamic equilibrium with active NA storage into cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2 (Eisenhofer et al., 2004), increased NA uptake by NAT in response to increased NA autocrine following [Ca2+]i increases or overexcitation may increase free NA by facilitating the passive NA leakage from cytoplasmic vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dynamic equilibrium concept and the cited literature.

claim: The affinity of MAO-A for NA may be modifiable as MAO-A activity is Ca2+-dependent.
source: Furthermore, the affinity of MAO-A for NA may be modifiable as MAO-A activity is Ca2+-dependent (Cao et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cao et al., 2007.

claim: Neuronal activity in LC neurons is transiently increased by stress through activation of corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) receptor together with glutamate receptors.
source: Neuronal activity in LC neurons is transiently increased by stress (Valentino and Foote, 1988) through activation of corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) receptor (Valentino et al., 1983; McCall et al., 2015) together with glutamate receptors (Valentino et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Valentino and Foote, 1988; Valentino et al., 1983; McCall et al., 2015; and Valentino et al., 2001.

claim: Long-term overexcitation due to chronic stress ultimately causes degeneration of LC neurons.
source: Nevertheless, it is known that long-term overexcitation due to chronic stress ultimately causes degeneration of LC neurons (Kitayama et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kitayama et al., 2004.

claim: LC neurons invariably display spike-frequency adaptation.
source: LC neurons invariably display spike-frequency adaptation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The cumulative spike number increased nonlinearly in a saturation manner.
source: When the cumulative number of spikes was plotted against the elapsed time from the onset of the current pulse every 50 ms, the cumulative spike number increased nonlinearly in a saturation manner (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no significant difference in b between the two groups of spike trains.
source: Because there was no significant difference in b between the two groups of spike trains, the profile of the normalized cumulative spike number vs the elapsed time remains the same regardless of firing frequency, suggesting that spike-frequency adaptation occurs in the same way.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The spike-frequency adaptation observed was almost completely abolished by a blocker of α2-AR, atipamezole.
source: The spike-frequency adaptation observed was almost completely abolished by a blocker of α2-AR, atipamezole (Figure 1D and E), which subsequently largely decreased pulse-afterhyperpolarization (pulse-AHP) (Figure 1D and E, blue and red stars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Atipamezole largely decreased pulse-afterhyperpolarization (pulse-AHP).
source: The spike-frequency adaptation observed was almost completely abolished by a blocker of α2-AR, atipamezole (Figure 1D and E), which subsequently largely decreased pulse-afterhyperpolarization (pulse-AHP) (Figure 1D and E, blue and red stars).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Bath application of NA induced a GIRK-I in response to the ramp pulse.
source: Bath application of NA induced a GIRK-I in response to the ramp pulse (Figure 1H, red trace) whereas addition of atipamezole to NA almost completely abolished the NA-induced GIRK-I (Figure 1H, blue trace), showing that GIRK-I reversed at –97 mV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Addition of atipamezole to NA almost completely abolished the NA-induced GIRK-I.
source: Bath application of NA induced a GIRK-I in response to the ramp pulse (Figure 1H, red trace) whereas addition of atipamezole to NA almost completely abolished the NA-induced GIRK-I (Figure 1H, blue trace), showing that GIRK-I reversed at –97 mV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: GIRK-I reversed at –97 mV.
source: Bath application of NA induced a GIRK-I in response to the ramp pulse (Figure 1H, red trace) whereas addition of atipamezole to NA almost completely abolished the NA-induced GIRK-I (Figure 1H, blue trace), showing that GIRK-I reversed at –97 mV.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The amplitudes of the inward component of NA-induced GIRK-I were invariably larger than those of the outward component, consistent with the inwardly rectifying property of GIRK-I.
source: The amplitudes of the inward component of NA-induced GIRK-I were invariably larger than those of the outward component, consistent with the inwardly rectifying property of GIRK-I.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and I.

claim: Atipamezole significantly decreased the amplitudes of the inward and outward components.
source: Atipamezole significantly decreased the amplitudes of the inward and outward components (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: NA autocrine is likely to be caused following respective spikes in the LC neuron, and NA is accumulated around the LC neuron to activate α2-AR-coupled GIRK channels, to cause spike-frequency adaptation by enhancing AHP.
source: Taken together, NA autocrine is likely to be caused following respective spikes in the LC neuron, and NA is accumulated around the LC neuron to activate α2-AR-coupled GIRK channels, to cause spike-frequency adaptation by enhancing AHP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figure 1.

claim: In PC12 cells, heterologously expressed α2A-ARs undergo internalization following agonist application.
source: In PC12 cells, heterologously expressed α2A-ARs undergo internalization following agonist application (Taraviras et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Taraviras et al., 2002.

claim: In LC neurons, NA-induced GIRK-I showed almost no rundown/desensitization after repeating the ramp pulse 20 times in the persistent presence of NA.
source: However, in LC neurons, NA-induced GIRK-I showed almost no rundown/desensitization after repeating the ramp pulse 20 times in the persistent presence of NA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Acute/chronic stress increases the excitability of LC neurons.
source: Then, we next examined whether GIRK-I shows rundown under the condition of 'increased excitability' or increased [Ca2+]i, because acute/chronic stress increases the excitability of LC neurons (Borodovitsyna et al., 2018; Campos-Lira et al., 2018) and various channels/receptors are known to be internalized in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Beattie et al., 2000; Aziz et al., 2012; Zaccor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Borodovitsyna et al., 2018 and Campos-Lira et al., 2018.

claim: Various channels/receptors are known to be internalized in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: Then, we next examined whether GIRK-I shows rundown under the condition of 'increased excitability' or increased [Ca2+]i, because acute/chronic stress increases the excitability of LC neurons (Borodovitsyna et al., 2018; Campos-Lira et al., 2018) and various channels/receptors are known to be internalized in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Beattie et al., 2000; Aziz et al., 2012; Zaccor et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beattie et al., 2000; Aziz et al., 2012; and Zaccor et al., 2020.

claim: α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I displayed Ca2+-dependent rundown in the presence of agonist.
source: α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I displayed Ca2+-dependent rundown in the presence of agonist.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The degree and time course of rundown of α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I were dependent on the number and timing of positive pulses applied under voltage-clamp condition to cause Ca2+ currents.
source: The degree and time course of rundown of α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I were dependent on the number and timing of positive pulses applied under voltage-clamp condition to cause Ca2+ currents (Figure 2A–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–J, Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and its supplements.

claim: It is likely that NA-induced GIRK-I displays a marked rundown in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: Thus, it is likely that NA-induced GIRK-I displays a marked rundown in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Intracellular barbadin effectively suppressed the rundown of GIRK-I.
source: In the present study, intracellular barbadin effectively suppressed the rundown of GIRK-I (Figure 2G–K), indicating that the rundown of GIRK-I was caused by the internalization of α2A-ARs in LC neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G–K.

claim: The rundown of GIRK-I was caused by the internalization of α2A-ARs in LC neurons.
source: In the present study, intracellular barbadin effectively suppressed the rundown of GIRK-I (Figure 2G–K), indicating that the rundown of GIRK-I was caused by the internalization of α2A-ARs in LC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the barbadin experiment shown in Figure 2G–K.

claim: Chronic cold stress reduced α2-AR-mediated inhibition of LC neurons.
source: Chronic cold stress reduced α2-AR-mediated inhibition of LC neurons (Jedema et al., 2008), and chronic social stress downregulated α2-ARs in the LC (Flügge, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jedema et al., 2008.

claim: Chronic social stress downregulated α2-ARs in the LC.
source: Chronic cold stress reduced α2-AR-mediated inhibition of LC neurons (Jedema et al., 2008), and chronic social stress downregulated α2-ARs in the LC (Flügge, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Flügge, 1996.

claim: Following RS, α2A-AR expression was decreased due to the internalization of α2A-ARs.
source: Our present results were consistent with those previous findings: Following RS, α2A-AR expression was decreased due to the internalization of α2A-ARs (Figure 3), together with the decreases in NA-induced GIRK-I (Figure 4A–G) which mediates the autoinhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There were decreases in NA-induced GIRK-I which mediates the autoinhibition.
source: Our present results were consistent with those previous findings: Following RS, α2A-AR expression was decreased due to the internalization of α2A-ARs (Figure 3), together with the decreases in NA-induced GIRK-I (Figure 4A–G) which mediates the autoinhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–G.

claim: As long as RS persists, the impairment of autoinhibition leads to the persistent overexcitation in LC neurons.
source: As long as RS persists, the impairment of autoinhibition leads to the persistent overexcitation in LC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Under chronic RS, the increased autocrine-released NA is directly and more rapidly taken up by NAT due to the absence of α2A-ARs.
source: As extracellular NA is mostly taken up into cytosol by NAT (Torres et al., 2003), it is likely that under chronic RS, the increased autocrine-released NA is directly and more rapidly taken up by NAT due to the absence of α2A-ARs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 6B.

claim: VMAT2 has a much higher affinity for NA than MAO-A.
source: After reuptake of NA by NAT, a large portion of NA in the cytosol is restored in cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2, while only a small portion of NA can escape from VMAT2 to be metabolized by MAO-A (Eisenhofer et al., 1992), because VMAT2 has a much higher affinity for NA than MAO-A (Bloom, 2006; Costa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bloom, 2006 and Costa et al., 2012.

claim: When reuptake of NA by NAT is facilitated due to the internalization of α2A-ARs in response to NA autocrine, active NA storage into cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2 would increase.
source: When reuptake of NA by NAT is facilitated due to the internalization of α2A-ARs in response to NA autocrine, active NA storage into cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2 would increase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: The rate of NA leakage from cytoplasmic vesicles would also increase because passive NA leakage from cytoplasmic vesicles and active NA storage into cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2 are in a dynamic equilibrium in cytoplasmic vesicles.
source: Then, the rate of NA leakage from cytoplasmic vesicles would also increase because passive NA leakage from cytoplasmic vesicles and active NA storage into cytoplasmic vesicles by VMAT2 are in a dynamic equilibrium in cytoplasmic vesicles (Eisenhofer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the dynamic equilibrium concept and citation to Eisenhofer et al., 2004.

claim: Such increases in the rate of NA leakage would result in increases in a MAO-A metabolite, DOPEGAL.
source: Subsequently, such increases in the rate of NA leakage would result in increases in a MAO-A metabolite, DOPEGAL (Goldstein, 2021; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed mechanism and citation to Goldstein, 2021.

claim: A partial inhibition of NAT in human subjects reduced the original level of a derivative of DOPEGAL (3,4-dihydroxyphenylglycol) in CSF by more than 50%.
source: Indeed, it has previously been demonstrated that a partial inhibition of NAT in human subjects reduced the original level of a derivative of DOPEGAL (3,4-dihydroxyphenylglycol) in CSF by more than 50% (Kielbasa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kielbasa et al., 2015.

claim: Free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A would be increased when autocrine-released NA is taken up by NAT.
source: Thus, free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A would be increased when autocrine-released NA is taken up by NAT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: The decreased VMAT2 levels, generated in VMAT2 heterozygote mice, increased the vulnerability of nigral dopamine neurons to MPTP.
source: On the other hand, it is also known that the decreased VMAT2 levels, generated in VMAT2 heterozygote mice, increased the vulnerability of nigral dopamine neurons to MPTP (Takahashi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takahashi et al., 1997.

claim: NA leakage for free NA accumulation is influenced by both NAT and VMAT2.
source: Thus, it is conceivable that NA leakage for free NA accumulation is influenced by both NAT and VMAT2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of NAT and VMAT2 roles.

claim: DOPEGAL converts pro-AEP into active-AEP to produce tau N368 protein.
source: Subsequently, DOPEGAL converts pro-AEP into active-AEP to produce tau N368 protein (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G–I.

claim: 5-day RS induced spatial memory impairment-like responses in mice when assessed using Y-maze test.
source: Indeed, 5-day RS induced spatial memory impairment-like responses in mice when assessed using Y-maze test (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) while anxiety-like behavior was also induced in mice after 3-day RS when assessed using an elevated plus maze test (figure not shown), both suggesting an impairment of LC neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anxiety-like behavior was also induced in mice after 3-day RS when assessed using an elevated plus maze test.
source: Indeed, 5-day RS induced spatial memory impairment-like responses in mice when assessed using Y-maze test (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) while anxiety-like behavior was also induced in mice after 3-day RS when assessed using an elevated plus maze test (figure not shown), both suggesting an impairment of LC neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text but the figure is not shown.

claim: In addition to NAT inhibitor, the suppression of the internalization of α2A-AR has a strong translational potential for developing drugs that prevent the degeneration of LC.
source: It is likely that, in addition to NAT inhibitor, the suppression of the internalization of α2A-AR has a strong translational potential for developing drugs that prevent the degeneration of LC.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: A stringent autoinhibition together with potent NAT activity was previously demonstrated in adult rats using intracellular recordings.
source: However, a stringent autoinhibition together with potent NAT activity was previously demonstrated in adult rats using intracellular recordings (Williams et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Williams et al., 1985.

claim: Spike-frequency adaptation reflecting autoinhibition can be induced in adult mice as prominently as in juvenile mice regardless of sexes.
source: We also confirmed that spike-frequency adaptation reflecting autoinhibition can be induced in adult mice as prominently as in juvenile mice regardless of sexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), although we did not investigate the sex differences in RS effects (Leistner and Menke, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reuptake of NA by NAT in LC neurons may decrease with age.
source: It has also been reported that reuptake of NA by NAT in LC neurons may decrease with age (Sanders et al., 2005; Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanders et al., 2005 and Mitchell et al., 2017.

claim: NAT expression in LC in 3-week-old juvenile mice was only slightly larger (by 4%) than in adult mice.
source: However, NAT expression in LC in 3-week-old juvenile mice was only slightly larger (by 4%) than in adult mice, although the difference was significant (Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2017.

claim: Partial inhibition of NAT in human subjects largely reduced the original level of a derivative of DOPEGAL in CSF.
source: Furthermore, partial inhibition of NAT in human subjects largely reduced the original level of a derivative of DOPEGAL in CSF as described above.
evidence: This refers back to the earlier citation to Kielbasa et al., 2015.

claim: Increased reuptake of NA by NAT following excessive NA autocrine in the absence of α2A-AR, induced in response to chronic RS, resulted in the increase in active-AEP and subsequent production of tau N368.
source: Thus, based on the present study, it is likely that increased reuptake of NA by NAT following excessive NA autocrine in the absence of α2A-AR, induced in response to chronic RS, resulted in the increase in active-AEP and subsequent production of tau N368.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Chronic RS impaired the autoinhibition in LC neurons by inducing Ca2+- and agonist-dependent internalization of soma/dendritic α2A-AR coupled with GIRK channels.
source: Our study unveiled the cellular mechanism for the degeneration of LC neurons under chronic RS as follows: Chronic RS impaired the autoinhibition in LC neurons by inducing Ca2+- and agonist-dependent internalization of soma/dendritic α2A-AR coupled with GIRK channels.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Impairment of autoinhibition subsequently caused overexcitation/[Ca2+]i increases and increased Ca2+-dependent MAO-A activity and active AEP activity, leading to a production of tau N368 fragment together with an impairment of spatial memory.
source: This subsequently caused overexcitation/[Ca2+]i increases and increased Ca2+-dependent MAO-A activity and active AEP activity, leading to a production of tau N368 fragment together with an impairment of spatial memory.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Chronic RS increases cytosolic free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A, presumably by facilitating the reuptake of autocrine-released NA due to the absence/internalization of α2A-AR.
source: These results clearly indicate that chronic RS increases cytosolic free NA to be metabolized by MAO-A, presumably by facilitating the reuptake of autocrine-released NA due to the absence/internalization of α2A-AR.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: LC neurons expressed much higher mRNA level of α2A-AR than that of α2C-AR.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that LC neurons expressed much higher mRNA level of α2A-AR than that of α2C-AR (Figure 4H) and also expressed higher mRNA level of GIRK1 compared to GIRK2 while GIRK3 was hardly expressed (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: LC neurons expressed higher mRNA level of GIRK1 compared to GIRK2 while GIRK3 was hardly expressed.
source: Quantitative PCR analysis revealed that LC neurons expressed much higher mRNA level of α2A-AR than that of α2C-AR (Figure 4H) and also expressed higher mRNA level of GIRK1 compared to GIRK2 while GIRK3 was hardly expressed (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: mRNA levels of α2A-AR, GIRK1, and GIRK2 in mice subjected to 3-day RS were significantly smaller than those of the control mice.
source: Consistent with the significant decreases in NA-induced GIRK-I in the mice subjected to 3-day RS, mRNA levels of α2A-AR, GIRK1, and GIRK2 in mice subjected to 3-day RS were significantly smaller than those of the control mice (Figure 4J–L).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4J–L.

claim: RS downregulated the expression/production of α2A-AR-coupled GIRK1 prominently in LC neurons.
source: Thus, RS downregulated the expression/production of α2A-AR-coupled GIRK1 prominently in LC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the qPCR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: 5-day RS appeared to slightly increase the expressions of TH and MAO-A in LC neurons.
source: Next, immunohistochemical experiments demonstrated that 5-day RS appeared to slightly increase the expressions of TH and MAO-A in LC neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AEP expression also appeared to increase in cytosol after 5-day RS compared to the control.
source: Furthermore, AEP expression also appeared to increase in cytosol after 5-day RS compared to the control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant increase in the protein level of TH was observed in 5-day RS mice compared to the control.
source: No significant increase in the protein level of TH was observed in 5-day RS mice compared to the control (Figure 5A, upper panel; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: TH activity was not significantly upregulated in 5-day RS mice.
source: This result clearly indicates that TH activity was not significantly upregulated in 5-day RS mice, in spite of the TH immunohistochemical experiment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blot data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed significant increases in the protein levels of MAO-A in LC neurons after 5-day RS compared to the control.
source: We further examined whether protein levels of MAO-A and AEP are increased or not by 5-day RS. Western blot analysis revealed significant increases in the protein levels of MAO-A (Figure 5A, lower panel; Figure 5C) and of pro-AEP and active AEP (Figure 5D–F) in LC neurons after 5-day RS compared to the control.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed significant increases in the protein levels of pro-AEP and active AEP in LC neurons after 5-day RS compared to the control.
source: We further examined whether protein levels of MAO-A and AEP are increased or not by 5-day RS. Western blot analysis revealed significant increases in the protein levels of MAO-A (Figure 5A, lower panel; Figure 5C) and of pro-AEP and active AEP (Figure 5D–F) in LC neurons after 5-day RS compared to the control.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D–F.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a significant increase in the expression of tau and tau N368 fragment after 5-day RS.
source: Western blot analysis also revealed a significant increase in the expression of tau and tau N368 fragment after 5-day RS (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G–I.

claim: An increased activity of active AEP caused a production of tau N368 fragments as observed at 37 and 35 kDa.
source: Thus, an increased activity of active AEP caused a production of tau N368 fragments as observed at 37 and 35 kDa (Figure 5G), which is consistent with a previous report (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G and citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: The two band intensities may reflect the two N-terminal fragments (upper and lower bands) generated by AEP cleavage at Asn-368 of the 4 and 3 repeat-tau isoforms, respectively.
source: Relative protein levels of the tau N368 fragments (Figure 5I) were the mean values obtained from the two band intensities, which may reflect the two N-terminal fragments (upper and lower bands) generated by AEP cleavage at Asn-368 of the 4 and 3 repeat-tau isoforms, respectively (Goedert et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an inference based on the western blot data and citation to Goedert et al., 1989.

claim: The Y-maze test revealed that 5-day RS decreased spatial memory.
source: Finally, the Y-maze test revealed that 5-day RS decreased spatial memory (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In non-stress mice, autocrine-released NA is slowly taken up by NAT after binding to α2A-ARs to cause autoinhibition.
source: In non-stress mice, autocrine-released NA is slowly taken up by NAT after binding to α2A-ARs to cause autoinhibition (Figure 6A), while in chronic RS mice, autocrine-released NA may be directly and rapidly taken up by NAT due to the absence (internalization) of α2A-ARs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In chronic RS mice, autocrine-released NA may be directly and rapidly taken up by NAT due to the absence (internalization) of α2A-ARs.
source: In non-stress mice, autocrine-released NA is slowly taken up by NAT after binding to α2A-ARs to cause autoinhibition (Figure 6A), while in chronic RS mice, autocrine-released NA may be directly and rapidly taken up by NAT due to the absence (internalization) of α2A-ARs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Such an increased rate of reuptake of NA by NAT would increase free NA concentration by facilitating the leakage of NA from cytoplasmic vesicles in the cell body, which would be metabolized by upregulated MAO-A activity to DOPEGAL, as revealed by the increased activity of AEP in chronic RS mice.
source: Such an increased rate of reuptake of NA by NAT would increase free NA concentration by facilitating the leakage of NA from cytoplasmic vesicles in the cell body, which would be metabolized by upregulated MAO-A activity to DOPEGAL, as revealed by the increased activity of AEP in chronic RS mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism shown in Figure 6B and is based on the experimental findings.

claim: The spike-frequency adaptation was mediated by α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I as the spike-frequency adaptation was abolished by atipamezole and by causing the rundown of GIRK-I.
source: In LC neurons, the spike-frequency adaptation was mediated by α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I as the spike-frequency adaptation was abolished by atipamezole (Figure 1D–G) and by causing the rundown of GIRK-I (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Autocrine NA release following respective spikes activated α2A-ARs expressed in the soma/dendrites of LC neurons and subsequently activated α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I to cause autoinhibition as spike-frequency adaptation.
source: These results suggest that autocrine NA release following respective spikes activated α2A-ARs expressed in the soma/dendrites of LC neurons and subsequently activated α2A-AR-coupled GIRK-I to cause autoinhibition as spike-frequency adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Spike-frequency adaptation clearly reflects NA autocrine.
source: Thus, spike-frequency adaptation clearly reflects NA autocrine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Given the Ca2+ dependency of the rundown of autoinhibition, the excitability of LC neurons would increase as LC neurons were excited more such as under RS condition, resulting in a vicious cycle between excitability increase accompanied by [Ca2+]i increase and rundown of autoinhibition/Ca2+-dependent internalization of α2A-ARs.
source: Given the Ca2+ dependency of the rundown of autoinhibition, the excitability of LC neurons would increase as LC neurons were excited more such as under RS condition, resulting in a vicious cycle between excitability increase accompanied by [Ca2+]i increase and rundown of autoinhibition/Ca2+-dependent internalization of α2A-ARs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings about Ca2+-dependent rundown.

claim: Activation of GPCR by agonist binding usually causes the formation of GPCR/β-arrestin complexes.
source: Activation of GPCR by agonist binding usually causes the formation of GPCR/β-arrestin complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPCR signaling.

claim: The GPCR/β-arrestin complex is assembled through the interaction between β-arrestin and AP2 in clathrin-coated pits (CCPs), which is formed by the association of AP2 with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) at the plasma membrane, leading to endocytosis of GPCRs.
source: Subsequently, the GPCR/β-arrestin complex is assembled through the interaction between β-arrestin and AP2 in clathrin-coated pits (CCPs), which is formed by the association of AP2 with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) at the plasma membrane, leading to endocytosis of GPCRs (Pierce and Lefkowitz, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pierce and Lefkowitz, 2001.

claim: PIP2 is locally produced from the membrane phosphatidylinositol (PI) by PI4/PIP5 kinases in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: PIP2 is locally produced from the membrane phosphatidylinositol (PI) by PI4/PIP5 kinases in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Sarmento et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sarmento et al., 2014.

claim: Barbadin prevented the stable formation of sufficient GPCR/β-arrestin/AP2 complexes in CCPs as barbadin prevents AP2 from binding with β-arrestin by forming barbadin/AP2 complex, thereby hampering GPCR internalization.
source: Barbadin prevented the stable formation of sufficient GPCR/β-arrestin/AP2 complexes in CCPs as barbadin prevents AP2 from binding with β-arrestin by forming barbadin/AP2 complex, thereby hampering GPCR internalization (Beautrait et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beautrait et al., 2017.

claim: After the rundown of GIRK-I was observed in the voltage-clamp experiment, the spike-frequency adaptation was absent in the current clamp experiment, and the pulse-ADP was largely reduced.
source: To investigate the effects of the rundown of GIRK-I on the spike-frequency adaptation, spike trains were examined before and after the voltage-clamp experiment (Figure 2A–F). After the rundown of GIRK-I was observed in the voltage-clamp experiment, the spike-frequency adaptation was absent in the current clamp experiment, and the pulse-ADP was largely reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: The cumulative spike number that increased nonlinearly in a saturation manner before rundown of GIRK-I increased almost in a linear manner after rundown of GIRK-I.
source: The cumulative spike number that increased nonlinearly in a saturation manner before rundown of GIRK-I increased almost in a linear manner after rundown of GIRK-I (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E and F.

claim: The rundown of GIRK-I invariably resulted in an abolishment of spike-frequency adaptation, similar to the effects of atipamezole on spike-frequency adaptation.
source: Thus, the rundown of GIRK-I invariably resulted in an abolishment of spike-frequency adaptation, similar to the effects of atipamezole on spike-frequency adaptation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of data from Figures 1 and 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Ca2+ increases can cause the rundown of NA-induced GIRK-I and almost abolish the spike-frequency adaptation, leading to an increase in the excitability of LC neurons.
source: Therefore, it is likely that Ca2+ increases can cause the rundown of NA-induced GIRK-I and almost abolish the spike-frequency adaptation, leading to an increase in the excitability of LC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: NA-induced GIRK-I subjected to the combined command pulse 20 times in the presence of atipamezole was significantly restored after washout of atipamezole in the presence of NA.
source: We found that NA-induced GIRK-I subjected to the combined command pulse 20 times in the presence of atipamezole was significantly restored after washout of atipamezole in the presence of NA (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A–D.

claim: GIRK-I was not downregulated solely by [Ca2+]i increases without activation of α2-AR.
source: This observation indicates that GIRK-I was not downregulated solely by [Ca2+]i increases without activation of α2-AR, clearly revealing that both the activation of α2-AR and [Ca2+]i increases are necessary to cause the downregulation of GIRK-I.
evidence: This is an inference based on the atipamezole experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A–D.

claim: Both the activation of α2-AR and [Ca2+]i increases are necessary to cause the downregulation of GIRK-I.
source: This observation indicates that GIRK-I was not downregulated solely by [Ca2+]i increases without activation of α2-AR, clearly revealing that both the activation of α2-AR and [Ca2+]i increases are necessary to cause the downregulation of GIRK-I.
evidence: This is an inference based on the atipamezole experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A–D.

claim: The spike-frequency adaptation reflecting the autoinhibition was also preserved in spite of [Ca2+]i increases as long as activation of α2-AR is prevented.
source: In agreement with this result, the spike-frequency adaptation reflecting the autoinhibition was also preserved in spite of [Ca2+]i increases as long as activation of α2-AR is prevented (Figure 2—figure supplement 5E–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5E–J.

claim: GIRK channel blockade did not prevent the rundown of NA-induced GIRK currents following [Ca2+]i increases.
source: We further examined whether the rundown of NA-induced GIRK-I can be prevented by the presence of a GIRK channel blocker, tertiapin-Q. GIRK channel blockade did not prevent the rundown of NA-induced GIRK currents following [Ca2+]i increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A–H.

claim: The spike-frequency adaptation was not preserved by the blockade of GIRK channels during [Ca2+]i increases.
source: In agreement with this result, the spike-frequency adaptation was not preserved by the blockade of GIRK channels during [Ca2+]i increases (Figure 2—figure supplement 6I–N).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6I–N.

claim: α2-AR blockade but not GIRK blockade prevented the rundown of NA-induced GIRK-I following [Ca2+]i increases.
source: These findings showed that α2-AR blockade but not GIRK blockade prevented the rundown of NA-induced GIRK-I following [Ca2+]i increases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from Figure 2—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: The rundown of NA-induced GIRK-I may be brought about by the internalization of α2-AR in a Ca2+-dependent manner, regardless of opening or closing of GIRK channels.
source: Taken together, it is suggested that the rundown of NA-induced GIRK-I may be brought about by the internalization of α2-AR in a Ca2+-dependent manner, regardless of opening or closing of GIRK channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings from Figure 2 and its supplements.

claim: The immunoreactivity for α2A-ARs seen along the membrane of TH-positive LC neurons was apparently lower in RS mice compared to the control.
source: After mice were subjected to daily 12 hr RS for 3 days followed by non-stress condition for 2 days, the immunoreactivity for α2A-ARs (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1) seen along the membrane of TH-positive LC neurons was apparently lower compared to the control (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed significantly lower protein levels of α2A-ARs in LC neurons obtained after 3-day RS compared to the control.
source: Consistent with this observation, western blot analysis revealed significantly lower protein levels of α2A-ARs in LC neurons obtained after 3-day RS compared to the control (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The immunoreactivity for α2A-AR expression was apparently lower in LC neurons of RS mice than in those of the control mice in the membrane fraction.
source: Especially when α2A-AR expression was examined in the membrane fraction identified using Na+/K+-ATPase, the immunoreactivity for α2A-AR expression was apparently lower in LC neurons of RS mice than in those of the control mice (Figure 3D and E; *, compare the rightmost lower panels).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a significantly lower protein level of α2A-ARs in the membrane fraction of LC neurons of RS mice compared to the control.
source: Consistent with this observation, western blot analysis revealed a significantly lower protein level of α2A-ARs in the membrane fraction of LC neurons of RS mice compared to the control, whereas there was no significant difference in the cytosol between the control and RS mice (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: There was no significant difference in cytosolic α2A-AR levels between the control and RS mice.
source: Consistent with this observation, western blot analysis revealed a significantly lower protein level of α2A-ARs in the membrane fraction of LC neurons of RS mice compared to the control, whereas there was no significant difference in the cytosol between the control and RS mice (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: The internalization of α2A-ARs is not necessarily accompanied by increases in cytosolic levels of α2A-ARs because the internalized receptors are either recycled or degraded.
source: Thus, the internalization of α2A-ARs is not necessarily accompanied by increases in cytosolic levels of α2A-ARs because the internalized receptors are either recycled or degraded (Koenig and Ikeda, 1996; Takei et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and citations to Koenig and Ikeda, 1996 and Takei et al., 1996.

claim: NA-induced GIRK-I decreased with an increase in the RS period.
source: As 3-day RS caused the internalization or downregulation of α2A-ARs, we next examined if the daily 12 hr RS for up to 5 days can differentially cause reductions of NA-induced GIRK-I in LC neurons. NA-induced GIRK-I decreased with an increase in the RS period (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–E.

claim: The amplitudes of inward and outward components of GIRK-I decreased with the increase in the period of RS in a way that is described by a saturation function.
source: The amplitudes of inward and outward components of GIRK-I decreased with the increase in the period of RS (Figure 4F and G), in a way that is described by a saturation function (red interrupted lines).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The amplitudes of inward and outward components of GIRK-I in 1-day mice were significantly smaller than those of the control mice.
source: The amplitudes of inward and outward components of GIRK-I in 1-day mice were significantly smaller than those of the control mice, and those in 3-day RS mice were significantly smaller than those in 1-day RS mice, while there was no significant difference in those between 3-day and 5-day RS mice (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The amplitudes of GIRK-I in 3-day RS mice were significantly smaller than those in 1-day RS mice.
source: The amplitudes of inward and outward components of GIRK-I in 1-day mice were significantly smaller than those of the control mice, and those in 3-day RS mice were significantly smaller than those in 1-day RS mice, while there was no significant difference in those between 3-day and 5-day RS mice (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: There was no significant difference in GIRK-I amplitudes between 3-day and 5-day RS mice.
source: The amplitudes of inward and outward components of GIRK-I in 1-day mice were significantly smaller than those of the control mice, and those in 3-day RS mice were significantly smaller than those in 1-day RS mice, while there was no significant difference in those between 3-day and 5-day RS mice (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The downregulation of GIRK-I was increased as the RS period was increased, but in a saturation manner.
source: Thus, the downregulation of GIRK-I was increased as the RS period was increased, but in a saturation manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4F and G.
